1	\begin{abstract}
2	Test-time compute scaling (repeated sampling with self-consistency or best-of-$N$) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning, but whether these gains transfer to named entity recognition (NER) remains open.
3	We characterize when scaling succeeds and fails, using NER (four datasets, primarily 7--14B fine-tuned) as the primary analysis, with preliminary cross-task pilots (relation extraction [RE], SQL).
4	Quality estimation signals predict output quality (area under the ROC curve [AUROC] up to $0.82$), yet instance-level selection yields no detectable gains (${<}1$ percentage point [pp]; confidence interval crosses zero), revealing a \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
5	A diagnostic framework identifies two co-occurring conditions, \textit{degeneracy} (i.e., multiple outputs collapsing to identical predictions) and signal alignment collapse, that are jointly associated with scaling returns; cross-task exploration confirms task-specific failure modes.
6	Entity-level construction yields conditional gains ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD under 3-epoch training; collapses at convergence; global Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.055$, suggestive; per-family $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.006$, post-hoc family partition) but exhibits inverse scaling in most configurations.
7	The framework is primarily diagnostic, with limited predictive power for identifying favorable conditions, informing resource allocation decisions before investing in repeated inference.
8	\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
Test-time compute scaling via repeated sampling yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning, but whether these gains transfer to named entity recognition (NER) remains open.
Across four NER datasets with fine-tuned 7--14B models, we find that quality estimation signals predict output quality well (area under the ROC curve [AUROC] up to $0.82$), yet selecting among candidates produces no detectable improvement over greedy decoding, even with 64 samples.
We term this disconnect the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} and trace it to two co-occurring conditions: \textit{degeneracy}, where multiple samples collapse to identical predictions, and \textit{signal alignment collapse}, where per-sample scores fail to discriminate quality within an instance.
Entity-level construction offers conditional gains ($+1.40$ percentage points [pp] on Few-NERD) where the framework identifies favorable conditions, but exhibits inverse scaling in most configurations.
Cross-task pilots on relation extraction (RE) and SQL parsing confirm task-specific failure modes.
The framework is primarily diagnostic, informing when repeated sampling helps for structured prediction and when greedy decoding remains the better default.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling, including self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}, and extended reasoning \cite{muennighoff2025s1}, has become a reliable strategy for improving reasoning accuracy: sample multiple candidates, estimate quality, select the best.
This approach succeeds when outputs admit equivalence classes or execution-based verification.
For NER, outputs are entity sets with partial overlap, and the boundary conditions for effective scaling remain unknown.
Prior work reports task-level correlations between consistency and accuracy \cite{yao2026consistency} and documents diversity collapse under constrained decoding \cite{yun2025price}, but neither provides instance-level diagnostics that explain \textit{when} scaling helps and \textit{when} it harms.

We study this question across four NER benchmarks and two model families (7--14B fine-tuned, with ablations to 72B), using RE as a secondary case study.
Our central finding is a \textbf{correlation-selection gap}: quality estimation (QE) signals predict output quality with strong discrimination (AUROC up to $0.82$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), yet using these signals to select among candidates yields no detectable improvement.
Majority vote (MV) gains remain below one percentage point (pp) even at $N{=}64$ (Figure~\ref{fig:n_scaling}; Table~\ref{tab:selection}), and log-probability (LP), the only per-sample signal, is neutralized by within-instance compression (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
The gap has structural roots: four of five signals assign identical scores to all candidates from a given input, so they estimate quality across inputs but cannot rank candidates within one.

A diagnostic framework traces these failures to two co-occurring conditions.
\textit{Degeneracy} ($12$--$68$\% of instances) produces identical outputs across all $N$ samples, eliminating any opportunity for selection.
\textit{Signal alignment collapse} ($\alpha{\to}0$, where $\alpha$ denotes LP-F1 alignment) renders LP an unreliable guide even on non-degenerate instances; a bound analysis (\S\ref{sec:theory}) confirms that alignment, not degeneracy, is the binding constraint ($8$--$33{\times}$ tighter).
A hidden-state probe reveals a related \textit{introspection boundary} \cite{huang2024large}: models encode entity quality internally (AUROC $0.63$--$0.88$; Appendix~\ref{sec:mechanistic}) but entity self-judgment (ESJ) achieves only chance-level discrimination (AUROC ${\approx}0.51$).
The framework is observational: it decomposes where failures occur post-hoc, without claiming causal mechanisms; all reported associations are correlational.

Exploratory entity-level construction yields conditional improvement ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}) where the framework identifies favorable conditions (low degeneracy, LP-F1 alignment), but inverse scaling in most $N$-transitions confirms that scaling is harmful in the majority of configurations.
The optimal strategy is dataset-dependent: LP selection on Few-NERD, MV on CoNLL.
These findings rest on four NER benchmarks, two model families with 4B--72B ablations, $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 64\}$, and exploratory extensions to RE\footnote{RE F1 is confounded by entity span errors: the majority of zero-F1 RE instances reflect upstream NER mismatches rather than relation classification failure (Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).} and SQL parsing ($87.2$\% degeneracy).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap (diagnostic sequence, not causal chain). Representative values across datasets: AUROC from CoNLL EM; $\rho$ and entity-construction gain from Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$; Tables~\ref{tab:multiseed},~\ref{tab:entity_construction}). \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality. \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: LP-weighted entity construction ($\theta{=}2/N$) yields conditional gains ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

Our investigation proceeds in three stages:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
\item \textbf{Discover} [\S\ref{sec:qe_results}].
QE signals achieve strong instance-level discrimination (AUROC up to $0.82$); while \citet{yao2026consistency} report task-level correlation, our instance-level decomposition reveals why this does not translate into selection gains.
\item \textbf{Diagnose} [\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:adaptive}, \S\ref{sec:theory}].
A diagnostic cascade quantifies failure mechanisms at entity level; \citet{yun2025price} describe diversity collapse qualitatively, we provide quantitative decomposition through degeneracy ($D$), alignment ($\alpha$), and LP range. A necessary condition bound confirms $\alpha$ as the binding constraint (3--12\% recovery ratio). Hidden-state probes expose an introspection boundary (probe AUROC up to $0.88$ vs.\ ESJ ${\approx}0.50$; Appendix~\ref{sec:mechanistic}).
\item \textbf{Construct (exploratory)} [\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}].
Entity-level construction yields $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD where the cascade identifies favorable conditions, but inverse scaling dominates most configurations. Unlike \citet{xie2023zeroshot}'s zero-shot entity voting, we aggregate stochastic samples from fine-tuned models.
\end{enumerate}

The paper is organized as follows: \S\ref{sec:related} contextualizes our contributions; \S\ref{sec:method} defines the diagnostic framework; \S\ref{sec:selection_gap} establishes the correlation-selection gap; \S\ref{sec:adaptive} evaluates adaptive methods; \S\ref{sec:theory_scaling} provides scaling analysis; \S\ref{sec:experiments} presents cross-dataset results.
